questions.question: Antoine Lavoisier suspected that breathing is a slow burning of carbon. With Pierre-Simon Laplace, in the winter of 1782 to 1783, he shut a guinea pig for ten hours in a chamber packed round with ice, weighed the water from the ice its body heat melted, and measured the fixed air, now called carbon dioxide, that it breathed out. They burned charcoal in such a chamber too. Which result would back Lavoisier's idea?
questions.answer: About the same ice for each ounce of fixed air as charcoal melts
choices: About the same ice for each ounce of fixed air as charcoal melts
Far less ice for each ounce of fixed air, as breathing is so slow
About the same ice for each hour as a lump of burning charcoal
Far more ice for each hour than a lump of burning charcoal
questions.context: The guinea pig melted about 13 ounces of ice in ten hours, and charcoal giving off as much fixed air melts about 10, as close a match as Lavoisier could hope for, so he wrote that respiration is a combustion, very slow but like the burning of carbon. Burning the same amount of carbon gives the same heat whether it goes slowly or fast, so the fair test is per ounce of fixed air, not per hour: charcoal burns far faster than a guinea pig breathes. Aristotle and Galen had taught that breathing cools the blood; the slow burning is now known to run, step by step, in the mitochondria of the body's cells.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches cellular respiration as a slow, controlled burning of fuel, and Lavoisier's ice calorimeter is the classic first measurement of it.

questions.question: In cellular respiration, glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water, and the energy released is stored in a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). A runner breathes in oxygen with every stride and breathes out carbon dioxide. In the reactions of respiration, where do the atoms of the oxygen she breathes in end up?
questions.answer: In the water made in the mitochondria
choices: In the water made in the mitochondria
In the carbon dioxide she breathes out
In the ATP made in the mitochondria
In the glucose stored in her cells
questions.context: At the end of the chain of reactions on the inner membrane of the mitochondria, each oxygen molecule takes up electrons and hydrogen ions and becomes water; it is the only step in breaking down glucose that uses the oxygen breathed in. The carbon dioxide breathed out is built from the glucose's own carbon, split off in the mitochondria, and no oxygen gas goes into ATP or glucose. Respiration runs roughly as photosynthesis in reverse, which splits water and gives its oxygen off as gas.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology traces the reactants of respiration through to its products, and where the oxygen ends up is the standard check that the equation is understood, not memorised.

questions.question: Louis Pasteur grew yeast in flasks of sugar solution in the late 1850s. Air bubbled through a flask made the yeast grow faster and ferment less; shut away from air, it fermented hard and used up its sugar much faster. A cell stores the energy it frees from sugar in a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Why does yeast without oxygen go through so much more sugar?
questions.answer: Each sugar yields far less ATP without oxygen
choices: Each sugar yields far less ATP without oxygen
Each sugar yields its ATP more slowly without oxygen
Its enzymes are used up faster without oxygen
It splits sugar to free the oxygen it lacks
questions.context: Fermenting a molecule of glucose yields only 2 ATP, while respiring it fully with oxygen in the mitochondria yields many times more, about 30 in human cells and up to about 18 in yeast, so a yeast cell without air must break down far more sugar for the same energy. Enzymes are not used up, and fermentation frees no oxygen: it keeps the first steps of breaking down sugar running and gives off alcohol and carbon dioxide. Biologists call oxygen's brake on fermentation the Pasteur effect.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology compares the ATP that respiration makes with and without oxygen, and Pasteur's yeast is the classic case of the difference at work.

questions.question: A girl runs her first long race, and two days later her legs ache more than ever. Until the 1980s, many blamed such aches on lactic acid, or lactate, which muscle cells make by fermentation when they run short of oxygen. Why do most exercise scientists now reject that idea?
questions.answer: It is back to normal within an hour, long before the ache peaks
choices: It is back to normal within an hour, long before the ache peaks
It stays in the leg muscles for days, yet causes no pain there
It forms only in the heart muscle, never in the muscles of the legs
It forms only in the muscles of runners who are out of training
questions.context: Blood lactate falls back to normal within about an hour after exercise, while the ache builds over the first day and is worst one to three days later; and exercise in which muscles shorten makes lactic acid too without leaving them sore. The ache comes instead from tiny tears in the muscle fibres, mostly in work where muscles lengthen as they pull, such as running downhill, and from the inflammation that follows: in a 1983 test, an easier downhill run left legs sore and a harder level run did not. Lactic acid does form in hard-working leg muscles, and the liver turns much of it back into fuel.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches lactic acid fermentation in muscle, and testing the soreness myth against the timing evidence is a standard exercise in judging a claim.

questions.question: Eduard Buchner ground yeast with quartz sand and squeezed out its juice under great pressure in 1897. Mixed with cane sugar, the juice gave off carbon dioxide for days, as living yeast does. Buchner said that a substance dissolved in the juice did the work, while followers of Louis Pasteur held that fermentation needs the living yeast cell. Which result would have counted most against Buchner?
questions.answer: Filtered of all its yeast cells, the juice did not ferment
choices: Filtered of all its yeast cells, the juice did not ferment
Boiled for a few minutes first, the juice did not ferment
Kept on ice for two weeks, the juice still fermented well
Given milk sugar in place of cane sugar, the juice did not ferment
questions.context: A few living cells slipping through the press would have explained everything, so juice passed through a filter that holds back every yeast cell was the deciding test; Buchner's filtered juice still fermented, and he named the dissolved agent zymase, a protein, winning the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Boiling, cold and a sugar the juice could not use fit either idea, since heat wrecks a protein as surely as it kills a cell. Zymase proved to be a team of enzymes that, in living yeast, does its work inside the cell.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that enzymes keep working outside the living cell, and Buchner's filtered yeast juice is the experiment that showed it.

questions.question: James Sumner crystallised urease, an enzyme from jack beans, in 1926 and found the crystals to be protein. Richard Willstätter, a Nobel Prize chemist, answered that Sumner had crystallised only a protein carrier, with the true enzyme, a much smaller molecule, clinging to it. John Northrop then crystallised pepsin, the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme, again and again. Which of his findings counted most against Willstätter?
questions.answer: Each gram kept the same activity through seven crystallisations
choices: Each gram kept the same activity through seven crystallisations
Each crystal kept the same shape through seven crystallisations
Each batch, dissolved again, still broke down other proteins
Each batch worked best in strong acid, as in a stomach
questions.context: If the true enzyme were a separate molecule merely clinging to a carrier, crystallising again and again should have shed some of it and changed the activity of each gram; Northrop found it steady, with the protein's makeup steady too, and concluded that pepsin itself is a protein. The crystals' shape and their power to digest protein in acid fit Willstätter's idea as well as Sumner's. The doubters gave way one by one, Willstätter last, and Sumner and Northrop shared the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Wendell Stanley.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that enzymes are proteins, and the dispute over Sumner's crystals shows how a test was found that could settle the question.

questions.question: Emil Fischer reported in 1894 on two forms of methyl glucoside, a compound of glucose. The two hold the very same atoms, joined in the same order, and differ only in which way one group points from the ring. An enzyme from yeast split one form and left the other untouched, while emulsin, an enzyme from almonds, split only the other. By Fischer's account, why could each enzyme split only one form?
questions.answer: Only that form fitted the enzyme's own shape
choices: Only that form fitted the enzyme's own shape
Only that form held its atoms loosely enough
Only that form dissolved readily enough in water
Only that form gave out energy as it was split
questions.context: Fischer wrote that an enzyme and the molecule it works on must fit together like a lock and its key, so turning a single group the other way was enough to shut one enzyme out and let the other in; if looseness, dissolving or energy had decided it, both enzymes would have split the same form. Daniel Koshland refined the picture in 1958 with induced fit: the enzyme's working pocket, its active site, is not rigid but closes snugly around the right molecule as it binds. That fit is why each enzyme is said to be specific to its own substrate.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches enzyme specificity through the lock-and-key and induced-fit models, and Fischer's two glucosides are where the idea began.

questions.question: A jar of dry glucose can sit on a laboratory shelf without changing, though glucose gives out a great deal of energy when it burns. Inside a cell at 37 degrees Celsius, with no flame, enzymes break glucose down in a chain of quick steps. How does an enzyme speed up its step?
questions.answer: It lowers the energy needed to start the step
choices: It lowers the energy needed to start the step
It supplies the energy needed to start the step
It raises the energy that the step gives out
It warms the molecules taking part in the step
questions.context: Every reaction, even one that gives out energy, needs a push to start, its activation energy; an enzyme offers an easier path with a far smaller push, so the step runs millions of times faster at body heat, and the enzyme itself comes out unchanged. It gives no energy of its own and leaves the energy the step gives out just as it was. Heating a cell enough to drive such reactions without enzymes would wreck its parts.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that enzymes speed reactions by lowering the activation energy, not by adding energy or heat.

questions.question: A man with the flu runs a fever of 39 degrees Celsius, a rise set by his brain that is thought to help him fight the virus. A body held at about 42 degrees or more, from heat stroke or an extreme fever, is in grave danger of brain damage and death. What goes wrong inside its cells at such a heat?
questions.answer: Their enzymes lose the shape their work depends on
choices: Their enzymes lose the shape their work depends on
Their enzymes are used up faster than new ones are made
Their water begins to boil away as steam
The germs inside them multiply faster than ever
questions.context: Heat shakes the folded chain of an enzyme loose, so its active site loses the shape that fits the molecules it works on; above about 40 degrees proteins begin to unfold, and held at 42 or more, cells and organs fail. A wrong pH bends enzymes out of shape in the same way, which is why each works best in its own range. Water boils only at 100 degrees and heat does not use enzymes up; a fever is a rise the brain sets on purpose, while heat stroke is the body's heat control failing.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches that heat and the wrong pH change an enzyme's shape, with a dangerously high body temperature as the standard example.

questions.question: Albert Szent-Györgyi found in 1933 that a small amount of fumarate or succinate, acids that cells make, sped up the oxygen use of minced pigeon breast muscle. The acid was not burned as fuel: the oxygen taken up far outran what so little acid could use. Hans Krebs and William Johnson found in 1937 that citrate did the same. What did Krebs conclude about these acids?
questions.answer: Each is remade at the end of a loop of reactions
choices: Each is remade at the end of a loop of reactions
Each is one step on a one-way chain of reactions
Each carries oxygen into the cells of the muscle
Each switches on enzymes that sat idle in the muscle
questions.context: Krebs and Johnson reasoned that an acid acting this way must be used up by one reaction and made again by a later one, so a little of it carries fuel round again and again; the loop, now called the citric acid or Krebs cycle, runs in the mitochondria and splits off carbon dioxide at each turn. A one-way chain would use up whatever acid was added to it, and these acids do not ferry oxygen. Nature turned down Krebs's short paper for lack of space, so it appeared in another journal, and he shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology introduces the Krebs cycle as the stage of respiration in the mitochondria, and the acids that were not used up are how a cycle was first inferred.
